hints: Compare the starting functional group with the product for each arrow, for example Br to OH means OH has replaced Br, while Br to C=C means HBr has been lost.
Recall the classic test for aqueous versus alcoholic NaOH with a halogenoalkane and what each solvent favours.
Think how a carbon chain can be extended by one carbon using cyanide, and how a nitrile can then be converted to a carboxylic acid.
Recall the two different oxidation products from a primary alcohol depending on conditions, aldehyde by distillation and carboxylic acid by vigorous oxidation.
Match each change to the allowed list, remembering hydrolysis means breaking by water, substitution means swap, elimination means loss of small molecule, oxidation means gain of O or loss of H.
Check that reaction 5 must stop at the aldehyde so it needs distillation, while reaction 6 goes to the acid so it needs stronger oxidising conditions.
walkthrough:
Read the carbon skeleton change**
Look at what is lost and gained. Reaction 1: $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{Br}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{OH}$. Only $\text{Br}$ swaps for $\text{OH}$, carbon count stays at 4. That is classic substitution, and because water or aqueous hydroxide supplies $\text{OH}$, it is also called hydrolysis.

Spot elimination versus substitution**
Reaction 2: $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{Br}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}=\text{CH}_{2}$. You lose $\text{HBr}$ and form $\text{C}=\text{C}$. Loss of a small molecule to form a double bond is elimination. You get this with $\text{OH}^{-}$ in ethanol, not water, because alcoholic conditions favour removal of $\text{H}^{+}$ from adjacent carbon.

Use cyanide to add a carbon**
Reaction 3: $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{Br}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. Chain grows from C4 to C5. Only $\text{CN}^{-}$ does this. Use $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ in ethanol, heat. $\text{CN}^{-}$ replaces $\text{Br}^{-}$, so it is still substitution.

Hydrolyse the nitrile to the acid**
Reaction 4: $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{COOH}$. The $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ becomes $\text{COOH}$ by adding water across the triple bond with acid catalysis. Use aqueous dilute $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ or $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$, heat. This is hydrolysis, also described as substitution.

Control oxidation of primary alcohol**
Reaction 5: $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{OH}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{2}\text{CHO}$. Primary alcohol to aldehyde is partial oxidation. You need acidified dichromate, $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$ with $\text{H}^{+}$, and you must distil off the aldehyde immediately so it is not oxidised further.

Oxidise aldehyde to acid**
Reaction 6: $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{2}\text{CHO}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{2}\text{COOH}$. Aldehyde to carboxylic acid is further oxidation. Use acidified $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ with heating under reflux, or Tollens, Fehlings or Benedicts reagent. This is oxidation.

Final answer: Reaction 1: aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{KOH}$ or water, heat; substitution / hydrolysis.
Reaction 2: ethanolic / alcoholic $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{KOH}$, heat; elimination.
Reaction 3: $\text{KCN}$ / $\text{NaCN}$ in ethanol / alcohol, heat; substitution.
Reaction 4: aqueous dilute $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ / $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$, heat; hydrolysis / substitution.
Reaction 5: acidified $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ / $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$ with $\text{H}^{+}$, distil; oxidation.
Reaction 6: acidified $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ / Tollens / Fehlings / Benedicts, heat; oxidation.

hints: Identify the nucleophile in reaction 1 and where its lone pair attacks, remembering SN2 is one step with attack and leaving in the same transition state.
Recall why the C-Br bond is polar and which direction the curly arrow for the bond breaking must point.
walkthrough:
Set up the nucleophilic attack**
Picture $\text{OH}^{-}$ approaching the carbon from the side opposite the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond. Oxygen has three lone pairs and a negative charge. Draw one lone pair on O and a curly arrow starting at that lone pair and pointing to the $\text{C}$ bonded to $\text{Br}$. At the same time show $\text{OH}^{-}$ with its negative charge.

Break the polar bond correctly**
Carbon is less electronegative than bromine, so the bond is $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. Mark those partial charges. Then draw a second curly arrow starting in the middle of the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond and pointing onto $\text{Br}$ to give $\text{Br}^{-}$. In SN2 both arrows occur together, forming $\text{RCH}_{2}\text{OH}$ in one step.

Final answer: Lone pair on O of $\text{OH}^{-}$ with curly arrow from lone pair to $\text{C}$ attached to $\text{Br}$.
$\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown with curly arrow from $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$ to form $\text{Br}^{-}$.

hints: Start from what stays the same in any isomers, think molecular formula and number of each atom.
Contrast structural with stereo by focusing on connectivity, how atoms are joined, not their arrangement in space.
Think of three ways connectivity can differ, the carbon skeleton, the position of a substituent, and the functional group itself.
Use 1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane as a mental example, same formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Br}$ but different skeleton and Br position.
walkthrough:
Define what is identical**
Both 1-bromobutane, $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{Br}$, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$, have formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Br}$. So start your definition there: same molecular formula, same numbers of atoms of each element.

Define what is different**
They are joined up differently. One has a straight four carbon chain with Br at the end, the other has a branched three carbon chain with Br in the middle. So they have different structural or displayed formulae, different connectivity.

Name the three families**
Chain or skeletal isomerism is different carbon skeleton, straight versus branched. Positional isomerism is same skeleton and functional group but different position, for example 1-bromobutane versus 2-bromobutane. Functional group isomerism is different functional group, for example an alcohol versus an ether with the same formula.

Final answer: Structural isomers are different molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural / displayed formulae.
Three types: chain / skeletal isomerism, positional / regioisomerism, functional group isomerism.

hints: Recall which mechanism primary halogenoalkanes favour and which mechanism tertiary halogenoalkanes favour.
Think about the intermediate formed when the C-Br bond breaks first on its own, and why a tertiary carbon stabilises a positive charge better.
Link stability to the number of alkyl groups and their electron donating inductive effect.
walkthrough:
Assign the mechanism**
Reaction 1 with 1-bromobutane, a primary halogenoalkane, goes by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ in one step. The tertiary isomer, $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$, is too hindered for backside attack and instead goes by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$, where $\text{Br}^{-}$ leaves first.

Picture the carbocation intermediate**
In $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$, ionisation gives $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+}$. A positively charged carbon is electron deficient. Alkyl groups push electron density towards it and spread the charge, lowering energy. Three methyl groups do this very effectively, so the tertiary cation is stable enough to form.

Contrast with the primary case**
If 1-bromobutane ionised it would give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$, with only one alkyl group attached to $\text{C}^{+}$. The $+\text{I}$ inductive donation is much smaller, the cation is high energy and does not form. So the primary compound avoids $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ and reacts by direct $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ attack instead.

Final answer: Mechanism: $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ / nucleophilic substitution unimolecular.
2-bromo-2-methylpropane forms a stable tertiary carbocation intermediate whereas 1-bromobutane cannot form a stable cation.
The tertiary cation is stabilised by three alkyl / methyl groups with greater $+\text{I}$ inductive electron donation, while the primary system has only one alkyl group and limited $+\text{I}$ effect.

hints: Recall how stereoisomers compare to structural isomers in terms of what stays the same, think connectivity.
Focus on what makes stereo special, the same connections but a different 3D orientation in space.
walkthrough:
Fix what is the same**
Imagine two models built with exactly the same bonds in the same order. Same molecular formula and same structural formula. That is the starting point for stereoisomers.

State what is different**
Now rotate or reflect one model. The atoms occupy different positions in space and the two forms cannot be interconverted without breaking bonds. That difference in 3D arrangement with identical connectivity is stereoisomerism.
Final answer: Stereoisomers have the same molecular and structural formula with the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement of atoms in space.

hints: Think of the two kinds of stereoisomerism at AS level, cis-trans about C=C and optical about a chiral carbon, and test but-1-ene for each.
Draw $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}=\text{CH}_{2}$ and look carefully at the groups attached to each end of the double bond.
walkthrough:
Test for optical isomerism**
Optical isomerism needs a chiral carbon with four different groups. But-1-ene, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}=\text{CH}_{2}$, has no such carbon. Any mirror image can be superimposed on the original, the molecule is achiral, so no optical isomers.

Test for cis-trans isomerism**
Cis-trans needs restricted rotation about $\text{C}=\text{C}$ plus two different groups on each carbon of the double bond. Here the $=\text{CH}_{2}$ end has two $\text{H}$ atoms, identical groups. Swapping them gives the same structure, so no cis-trans isomers exist.

Final answer: But-1-ene is achiral / has no chiral centre, its mirror images are superimposable.
One carbon of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond has two identical $\text{H}$ atoms attached so cis-trans isomerism is not possible.

hints: Write the addition of $\text{HCl}$ across $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}=\text{CH}_{2}$ and list the two possible places Cl can end up.
Recall which carbocation intermediate is more stable and therefore which chloroalkane is the major product X.
walkthrough:
Map the two addition routes**
Add $\text{H}-\text{Cl}$ across $\text{C}=\text{C}$. If $\text{H}$ adds to C1 and $\text{Cl}$ to C2 you get $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHClCH}_{3}$, 2-chlorobutane. If the reverse occurs you get $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$, 1-chlorobutane. These are positional structural isomers.

Pick major versus minor**
$\text{H}^{+}$ adds first to give the more stable secondary carbocation $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C}^{+}\text{HCH}_{3}$ rather than the primary cation. $\text{Cl}^{-}$ then attacks that cation. So 2-chlorobutane is formed in higher yield and is X, while 1-chlorobutane is Y.

Final answer: $\text{X}$ = 2-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHClCH}_{3}$.
$\text{Y}$ = 1-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{Cl}$ / $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$.

hints: Look at X, 2-chlorobutane, and check whether C2 is attached to four different groups.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centre in X**
In $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHClCH}_{3}$, carbon 2 is bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{Cl}$, $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, four different groups. That is a chiral centre, so X exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images, which is optical isomerism.
Final answer: Optical isomerism.

hints: Draw C2 of 2-chlorobutane with its four groups, using a solid wedge for a bond coming out and a hashed wedge for a bond going back.
To get the second stereoisomer, draw the exact mirror image or swap any two groups on the chiral carbon while keeping the other two fixed.
walkthrough:
Draw the first enantiomer clearly**
Put C2 in the centre. Show $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ with normal lines, $\text{Cl}$ with a solid wedge (out of the page) and $\text{H}$ with a hashed wedge (behind the page). Label all four groups so the tetrahedron is clear.

Draw its mirror image**
Draw the same skeleton but reflect it, for example keep $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ in place but swap $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{H}$ between wedge and dash. The two drawings must be mirror images that cannot be superimposed, representing the pair of optical isomers of X.

Final answer: One 3D structure of 2-chlorobutane with chiral C shown with wedge and dash bonds, e.g. central $\text{C}$ bonded to $\text{Cl}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$.
Second structure drawn as the non-superimposable mirror image, with two groups swapped relative to the first.
